guards.rule: An interior room camera must frame the room's defining functional group (a kitchen's run and island, a bedroom's bed) so the room reads as its type, not as a generic or secondary zone.
A scene check that reports a detached element must be re-run after the build stage so the element is re-attached to its room before the check is scored.
A scene check that reports a geometry failure must be re-run after the build stage so the offending geometry is corrected before the check is scored.
A site area labelled as a built outdoor space (veranda, balcony) must be built with its outline and structure, not left as an unrecognised open deck.

A stair piece must be assigned to a hall or dedicated stairwell room, never to a kitchen or other habitable room; the reading stage must re-assign a stair found inside a kitchen to the nearest hall or stairwell.
A furniture piece present in the decor stage must survive the agent stage; if it is dropped, the agent stage must be re-run to restore it.
A sink_kitchen piece must be built with a valid library model; if the current model is not built, swap to a valid model of the same type.
A door that must be shown in a view must be included in the view's show list so the camera frames it.
Drawings on the furniture layer that represent a sofa and chairs around a table must be read as furniture pieces, not lost.
A second label of a room that names a distinct space (ANTRE) must be read as a separate room, not as a second label of the existing room.
A dresser named in the documents must be read as a furniture piece in the model.
A bookshelf piece that is not built must be swapped to a valid library model of the same type.
An ottoman piece that is not built must be swapped to a valid library model of the same type.

A drawn nightstand that cannot be placed because the bed's footprint leaves no room is a layout conflict, not a reason to drop the piece: the furniture stage must re-solve the sleeping group (bed + nightstands) as one unit so the nightstand keeps its drawn place, rather than deleting it.

A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) that the documents outline must be built as a structured outdoor space (floor, guard on open edges, and a light roof where the plan shows one), not left as an unmodelled label.

A dressing room whose drawn wardrobe leaves no free span for the dressing group (mirror, bench) must have its wardrobe re-placed or the room re-typed so the defining pieces fit, rather than being left functionally empty.

A kitchen whose drawn counter run leaves no free span for the missing fridge (or whose relayout is blocked by the aisle rule) must have the counter run re-solved as one unit with the fridge included, rather than being left functionally empty.
A bathroom fixture listed in the room's pieces but absent from the render must be given a real library model (not a parametric mesh) so it is built and visible.
A bathroom camera that points at a corner and misses the primary fixtures (washbasin, toilet) must be re-aimed to show the main function of the space.
A bathroom camera that misses the primary fixtures (shower, toilet, basin) must be re-aimed to show the main function of the space.
A dressing room camera that cuts off the main furniture (wardrobes) and shows no defining pieces must be re-aimed to show the space's function.

A stair read into a kitchen (or any room where a stair does not belong) must be re-read as the missing kitchen fixture (fridge) if its size and position match, or removed if it is a misread symbol, rather than being left as a stair in the kitchen.
A door read from its lines (no swing arc) in an outer wall that is blocked by a drawn piece (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall that is blocked by drawn pieces (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A door read from its lines (no swing arc) in an outer wall that is blocked by drawn pieces (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A door read from lines without a swing arc in an outer wall, whose approach is blocked by furniture, is a window at the floor's sill, not a door.
A gap in an outer wall blocked by furniture is a window, not a door.
A wall cabinet must not be placed over a window; if no free wall span exists, it must be removed or the window moved.
Furniture must not cover a window opening.
Every room must be reachable from the entrance through doors, openings, or stairs.
Every floor must be reachable from the entrance.

A piece that blocks the ray through a window or door opening is a placement error: the fitting stage must keep the clear zone of every opening free of furniture, or move the piece to the nearest free spot.
A washbasin in a bathroom is always accompanied by a mirror above it; the bathroom_set group must include a mirror as a mandatory member.
A door leaf must be built with its frame and threshold at the correct floor level; a floating door leaf indicates a missing frame or a level mismatch in the door builder.
A site area marked 'NOT built (no outline)' that is referenced by a door or window in the plan must be built as an outdoor space with a floor slab and guard rails; the site stage must not skip it.
A kitchen must have a continuous run of base cabinets, wall cabinets, and appliances; the kitchen_run group must be placed as a single unit.
A door that opens onto an outdoor space must have that outdoor space built; the site stage must build the balcony or terrace before the door is placed.
The garden must include planted beds, shrubs, ground cover, and a path or parking area; the site stage must not leave it as bare flat grass.
A veranda or balcony marked 'NOT built (no outline)' must be built with a floor slab, guard rails, and a roof if drawn; the site stage must not skip it.
An entrance door must have a proper approach with steps, a landing, and cheek walls; the site stage must build the entrance solution.
A door that is blocked by furniture and has no outside passage is a reading error; it should be read as a window at the floor's sill height.
The pipeline must not end in 'pending' with recognition questions written; it must resolve all recognition questions before completing.
A washing machine's front must face a free side with at least 0.45 m clearance; the reading stage must verify the front direction against the room geometry.
A scene check failure for a built decor item must be resolved before the level is marked complete; the build stage must verify all decor items against the scene checks.
The big loop must run at least one full cycle before stopping; a zero-cycle stop with no gain is a failure to attempt, not a valid convergence.
Views marked for review must be resolved by the agent in the next round; a check finding is not a fix.
When a piece blocks a door or window and cannot be moved due to snap constraints, swap it for a narrower model that fits the available wall span.
When a TV unit cannot snap to a wall due to openings, swap for a model with a different depth or width that allows a valid placement.

When a bed model is rated as a 'crude placeholder' but higher-rated models are refused due to quality gates, swap for a generated model that offers better visual detail even if its library rating is lower, provided it fits the room.
Dressing rooms must include a dressing table or vanity group with accessories (mirror, stool, decor) to satisfy the 'styled surfaces' requirement; a wardrobe alone is insufficient.
Bedrooms should have a feature wall (e.g., slatted wood, paneling) behind the bed to add visual interest and match the reference style.
Nightstands in master bedrooms must be styled with accessories (books, vases, art) to avoid looking bare.
Living rooms must include a large area rug under the seating group to anchor the space.
Bedrooms should have a feature wall (e.g., paneling) behind the bed to add visual interest.
Bathroom cameras must show the main fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) to demonstrate the room's function and style.
Bathtub surrounds should use warm wood tones to match the project's aesthetic, not dark untextured panels.
Bathroom walls should use large-format porcelain tiles or stone to create a cohesive, high-end look, not flat cold white tiles.
Bathroom cameras must show the vanity unit and mirror to capture the room's style.
Kitchen cameras must show the kitchen run, island, and appliances, not just the dining nook.
Kitchen cameras must focus on the kitchen functional group, not the dining table.

A kitchen's program must include a styled-surface layer (small decor on the counter and island: a kettle, a fruit bowl, a cutting board) placed by the furniture agent, not only the functional run; a bare counter is a failed kitchen render.
A bathroom's program must include a mirror above the washbasin; a bare wall above the basin is a failed bathroom render.
A bedroom window's program must include a full-height two-layer curtain treatment (sheer behind a heavier drape) on a ceiling track; a single short sheer panel is a failed bedroom render.
A bedroom window's program must include a full-height two-layer curtain treatment (sheer behind a heavier drape) on a ceiling track; a single flat white panel is a failed bedroom render.
An interior camera of a small wet room must be posed from a free point with headroom that shows the room's main fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), never from a corner framing a wall and a door leaf.
A second interior view of a small room must frame the room as a whole, not a close-up of one fixture.
Two armchairs placed as a pair in one room must share a coherent style and palette; when they do not, swap the one that breaks the set to a model that matches its partner.

A piece listed in a room's program that is 'not built' must be built (or the room re-laid out) before the room is judged; a bare wall where a drawn work set belongs is a missing piece, not a styling gap.
An interior camera of a hall must show the hall's functional furniture (shoe cabinet, bench, console), not a bare blank wall.
A hall's entrance group is not complete with only a shoe cabinet; the furniture agent must add the missing styled layer (bench, hooks, mirror) that the reference shows.
An interior camera of a small hall must show the console and the space, not be jammed into the corner between the door and a wall.
A bed's layered bedding (duvet, second blanket, euro shams, decorative cushion) is a styling layer the furniture agent must add; a model swap that lowers the rating is not the fix.
Windows in a furnished bedroom must carry layered curtains (sheer plus drape on a track); bare windows are a missing styling layer the furniture agent must add.
Nightstands and dressers in a furnished bedroom must carry styled surfaces (vase, books, mirror, leaning art); bare tops are a missing styling layer the furniture agent must add.
An interior camera of a small room must show the room's main furniture and layout, not be pressed against a door and a wardrobe edge.
A second interior view of a small room must show the room and its furniture, not a close-up of a wall corner and door edge.

When a drawn piece is identified as a detail of a larger piece (e.g., a sink bowl or appliance front) but an AI pass names it as a distinct furniture type that fits its size, the reading stage must not discard it as a detail if the AI naming is plausible and the piece is not fully contained within the larger piece's functional zone.
The reading stage must process all entity types present in the source DWG file, including ATTDEF entities, to ensure no data is lost during the initial parsing phase.

The reading stage must correctly associate site decor elements with the appropriate level (L0 for ground floor site elements) and ensure that decor read outside the walls of upper levels is not duplicated or lost.

When a room outline holds multiple labels for distinct functional zones (e.g., 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading stage must split the room into separate entities if the labels represent distinct spaces with their own areas, rather than treating them as a single room with multiple labels.

Layers named after fixtures (e.g. 'DENIZLIK' for washbasin) that contain only line entities and no corresponding built fixture in the model should be checked: if the fixture is already built from another layer or source, the layer is redundant and the warning should be suppressed; if the fixture is missing, the layer's geometry should be used to place it.

When an opening is read twice (duplicate) and the build stage drops it, the build stage should check if the opening is a duplicate of an already-built opening (same wall, same position within tolerance). If it is a true duplicate, suppress the warning; if it is a distinct opening that was lost, rebuild it.

When decor elements are not built because their host piece is not built, the build stage should either (a) build the host piece, or (b) re-parent the decor elements to the room directly so they are built independently, or (c) explicitly mark them as not built with a clear reason. Silently dropping them is a loss.

Living rooms should include a rug under the seating area as part of the default decor set. The rug should be placed under the sofa and coffee table, sized to cover the seating group, and should not block door walkways.
Bathrooms with a washbasin should include a mirror over the washbasin as part of the default bathroom set. The mirror should be placed on the wall above the washbasin, centered, at a standard height.
A parametric opening in the style's finish is an acceptable build when no library model of the building's window family fits the opening's dimensions; it is not a defect.

When a piece is built with a parametric mesh because no library model fits, the fitting stage must record the piece's room and id so that a later swap_model or retype can target it; otherwise the library gap is unfixable by the agent.
A kitchen counter or island in a furnished render should carry at least one small appliance or decor item to avoid reading as an unfinished worktop.
A shower in a bathroom render should have a clear glass screen or proper tiling definition; a flat, untextured surface reads as a placeholder.
Nightstands in a bedroom should match the wood tone of the room's feature wall panelling to avoid introducing a clashing third wood tone.
A bedroom in a furnished render should have at least two layers of light (e.g., a statement fixture over the bed plus bedside lamps) to match the project's style.
Doors in a furnished render should have a wood tone and hardware that match the project's style; plain flat slabs with a single handle read as generic wardrobes.
A hall in a furnished render should have a rug to ground the space and add warmth, especially when the reference shows one.
Doors in a furnished render should have a wood tone and hardware that match the project's style; plain flat slabs in a pale wood read as generic placeholders.

A wardrobe model whose doors render as flat, untextured colour blocks is a low-quality asset: swap it for a library model of the same family with real door material, never move the piece to hide the look.

A facade that reads as flat planes with simple reveals needs a material with real surface breaks (render/plaster with texture, or a cladding) rather than a single flat colour; set the facade slot to a textured exterior look.

When a bedroom's TV unit has no suitable opposite wall for a media wall (due to openings, doors, or room shape), the TV unit should be repositioned to a side wall or removed if no valid placement exists, rather than leaving it in a position with no viewing wall.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished with its defining set (bench, full-length mirror, open storage or hanger rail); a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room and the room's program must be completed, not just re-modelled.
An interior camera must frame the room's layout and its main pieces, not be pressed against a door leaf or furniture edge at a low angle.
An exterior view must frame the main facade, entrance and the house's scale at eye level (1.5-1.7 m), not a corner of the roof and a hedge from too high and too far.
A scene check failure (S2) on a level means the build stage left a geometry inconsistency; the build stage must be re-run for that level.
A scene check failure (S3) on a level means the build stage left a geometry inconsistency; the build stage must be re-run for that level.
A furniture piece present in the decor stage must not be silently dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes or moves it, the record must name it.
A stove that is built into a kitchen counter run (a hob in the worktop) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.

A fridge that is built into a kitchen counter run (an integrated fridge in the run's fronts) is part of the counter module and does not need a separate scene object; the conservation check must not flag it as missing.
An exterior view that must show a window must frame the facade section containing that window; the camera position and target must be chosen so the window is in frame.

Drawings on the furniture layer ('tefriş') that depict a sofa or chairs around a table must be read as furniture pieces (sofa, chairs, table) and placed in the model; strokes on the furniture layer that no piece uses are lost furniture.

When the documents name a space (e.g. 'ANTRE') that is a second label of an existing room outline, the reading stage must split the room outline into two rooms if the documents show a wall or clear boundary between them; otherwise the space is lost.
A piece named in the documents (e.g. '*SIFONIYER' for a dresser) must be placed in the model at or near its named location; the furniture agent must add it if the reading did not.
A kitchen counter shown in the plan must be built in the model; if the kitchen run is incomplete, the furniture agent must complete it with the missing counter segments.

A drawn kitchen counter that the fit stage left unbuilt because it cut a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the kitchen run is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the counter is built, not dropped.

A standard bedroom-set piece (nightstand) that is left unbuilt because it cuts a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the sleeping group is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the nightstand is built, not dropped for a spatial conflict.

A decoration whose host piece is not built is a cascading loss: the build stage must either build the host (re-solving its group) or explicitly remove the decoration, never leave it dangling as 'not built'.
A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a bounded site area with its own floor and guard, not left as ad-hoc geometry with no outline.

A room's main group (dining table and its chairs) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main group is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A room's main piece (a hall's console table) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main piece is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A ray through a window opening must not hit furniture: the build stage must clear any piece that blocks the way through an opening.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a bare bowl with no mirror is a fundamental design failure.
A bathroom's washbasin must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the bathroom but misses the basin is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a basin with no mirror over it is a fundamental design failure.
A small enclosed room (under 3 m2) with no function, no pieces and no door of its own is most likely a misread: it is a hall or passage, not a room of its own, and must be typed accordingly.
A sliding door read from lines in an outer wall that is blocked by furniture across its approach and has no outside destination is a misread window: convert it to a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall that is blocked by furniture across its approach and has no outside destination is a misread window: convert it to a window at the floor's sill.
Furniture that covers a window opening must be moved to a free place in its room, clear of the opening.
Views marked for review must be re-evaluated in the next agent round after fixes are applied.

When a room's dining set is drawn but the solver cannot place it due to walkway constraints from doors, the drawn pieces should be kept as drawn and the walkway constraint should be relaxed for the dining zone, or the dining table should be moved to a position that satisfies both the walkway and the room's program.

When a kitchen's run is drawn but the solver cannot complete it due to missing appliances (fridge, hob), the drawn kitchen run should be kept as drawn and the missing appliances should be added as separate pieces, or the kitchen run should be re-solved with the missing appliances included.

When a bed_double blocks a door and cannot be moved due to overlap or plausibility constraints, the bed should be swapped for a smaller model (bed_single or a smaller bed_double) that fits the room and does not block the door, or the door should be moved to a different wall.
Every room must have a visible floor finish that matches the project's style.
The outdoor view through windows must show a believable environment with trees, ground cover, and site elements, not a low-poly placeholder.
A child's room must have wall art (murals, posters, or art) to match the reference style.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom must have a mirror over the basin to match the reference style.
A bathtub's model must match the project's light, minimalist aesthetic.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood textures, a vanity unit, a mirror, and a towel rail to match the project's style.
Kitchen renders must show styling and 'lived-in' layers to match the reference, not a raw architectural model.

A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a cohesive, age-appropriate set (playful, warm, child-sized); a generic adult office or minimalist set is a mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping the models to a matching style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a generic adult bedroom is a failure of the furniture set, not the camera.
A modern white office chair is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate chair that matches the room's style.
A minimalist white-framed office desk is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate desk that matches the room's style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a cluttered adult bedroom with clashing furniture is a failure of the furniture set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a wall showing a bare corner is a bad camera.
A nightstand in a master bedroom must match the room's warm, organic style; a loud, artificial object (e.g. a neon lamp) that clashes with the natural wood and neutral palette is a mismatch.
An armchair in a master bedroom must match the room's organic, boho style; a mid-century modern piece that clashes with the natural wood elements is a mismatch.
A render of a master bedroom must show a warm, organic, and layered interior; a sterile, unfinished shell with clashing surfaces is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A master bedroom must be lit with warm, cozy light; a flat, cool ambient light that feels like a hospital ward is a failure of the lighting and material set.
A render of a hall must show a warm, textured, and functionally styled interior; a bare, empty shell with no console table or decor is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A hall must have styled surfaces (console table, decor, and a rug); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a door leaf is a bad camera.
A storage room must have styled surfaces (hanging clothes, a mirror, etc.); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A bedroom under 12 m2 that the solver cannot relayout still gets one potted_plant in a corner the solver leaves free, so the room is never rendered bare.
When the current bed model is a blocky placeholder and a generated model of the same type and style is available, swap to the generated model rather than leaving the placeholder.
A bedroom render that shows only blocky furniture and flat walls is a fit failure: the furniture agent must add at least one plant, one textile and one wall item before the view is scored.
An interior camera that frames only a door and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe is missing its program: the furniture agent must add a mirror, a bench and wall art so the room reads as a dressing room, not a storage closet.
A room whose walls are completely bare in the render is missing the wall-art layer: the furniture agent must add at least one framed piece on a free wall span.
An interior camera that frames only a wall corner and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A facade that renders as a flat white box is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look (wood, stone, or brick) that matches the project's reference style.
A ground-floor plinth with no planters, shrubs or ground cover is a site failure: the site must include planters and a hedge or fence to soften the transition to the lawn.
A facade that renders as a bare clay model is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A facade that renders as a flat untextured white surface is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
An exterior wall with no place to sit is a site failure: the site must include a patio set or bench to make the exterior feel lived-in.
An exterior wall with no lanterns, wall sconces or path lights is a site failure: the site must include exterior lighting to define the space at night.
A facade that renders as a grey-box massing study is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A house with outside doors but no library entrance door is a build failure: the build stage must assign a statement entrance door model to the entrance opening.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a chair in the salon) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a shoe cabinet in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (a desk in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an office chair in the room) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.
A drawn piece the reading typed from the plan (an unknown item in the hall) must be built in the model; the furniture stage must not drop a drawn piece that fits its room.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between them (a wall not read) so each label keeps its own room; the label with the largest printed area is kept only as a fallback.
A room's furniture must read as a designed space, not a collection of pieces; the furniture stage must keep the room's function clear (a bedroom is not an office).
A piece must look like its type in every view; the fit stage must choose a model whose silhouette matches the type (a bed_double must not read as a bed_single).
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position.
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place and match its drawn size; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position and size.
A dressing room (Soyunma Odası) must contain at least a mirror and a bench or seating in addition to a wardrobe to be functionally complete; a single wardrobe is insufficient for the room type.

When a drawn furniture label (e.g., 'SIFONIYER' for dresser) is present in the documents but no corresponding drawn piece is found within 1 m of the label, the system should attempt to place the furniture at the label's location if the space is free, or flag it for manual review if the space is obstructed.

Elevation checks must be able to run even if the north arrow is missing, by using the plan's orientation or a default bearing, or by flagging the missing north arrow as a critical error that blocks the check.

When a drawn section does not align one-to-one with the plan (e.g., due to roof overhangs or section cuts), the check should either adjust the comparison to account for the offset or flag the misalignment for manual review.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: Elevations must have a view bearing or side assigned to them to allow comparison with the model; if missing, the system should infer the bearing from the plan or flag the elevation as incomplete.

When an interior door is drawn as a double and the library holds no double-leaf model, build it parametric in the style's finish and record a library_gap; do not force a single-leaf model onto a double opening.

A piece whose room is None (orphaned, not assigned to a room) cannot be refitted or swapped; the fitting stage must assign every placed piece to a room before the library-quality check, or the check must skip orphaned pieces instead of flagging them.

When two interior doors in the same tight space (hall, corridor) are built from the same heavy traditional model, the fitting stage should vary at least one to a lighter or different-style model from the library to avoid a dated, repetitive look.

When an opening is read twice (duplicate evidence) and is wide (>= 1.8 m), the build stage must build it as a single opening (or a double door) rather than dropping it; duplicate reads of the same opening should be merged, not discarded.

When a host piece is not built (e.g., removed or not placed), its attached decor elements should either be re-parented to a valid host or built independently if they are standalone items; the build stage should not silently drop decor just because its host is missing.
When a section prints a floor level offset from the plan's 0.00 datum, treat the plan's 0.00 as the finished-floor reference and ignore the section's offset for level assignment.
Small drawn pieces adjacent to level-mark text are symbols, not furniture; move them to the symbol layer.
Furniture name texts in the drawing confirm the presence of the named piece; no action needed if the piece is already built.
Zone labels in the drawing confirm the presence of the named zone; no action needed if the zone's furniture is already built.
Small seat-sized pieces adjacent to a dining table are chairs; type them by context.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked by a door or wall, and no alternative orientation is free, keep the inferred front.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked and no alternative model fits, keep the inferred front.
When an armchair's inferred front is blocked and no alternative orientation is free, keep the inferred front.

When a furniture name text in the drawing names a piece that is not drawn at that location, and the nearest valid place is more than 1 m away, add the piece at the text's location if it fits the room's program, or flag it for review if it does not.
When a door in the outer wall is blocked by a drawn piece, and the piece is not a door or a window, read the opening as a window at the floor's sill height.
An outer-wall opening whose approach is fully blocked by a drawn counter or fixture is a window, not a door: the reading must classify it by what stands in front of it, not by its width.
A wall unit must not stand over a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the unit to a free wall span.
A piece must not cover a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the piece to a free spot.
A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the plan must be built as a distinct site element with a floor slab and railing/outline, not left as an unrecognised open space.
A room typed as 'hall' with an area less than 3 m2 and no circulation function should be re-typed as 'storage' or 'other'.
Stairs should not be assigned to a kitchen room; they belong in a hall, stairwell, or circulation space.
A labelled veranda, terrace or balcony in the site plan must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, floor and railing, not dropped as 'no outline'.

A living room with a seating group must include a rug under the coffee table and sofa.
A bathroom with a washbasin must include a mirror above it.
Site areas labeled as 'BALKON' or 'VERANDA' in the plan must be built as functional outdoor rooms with floors, guards on open edges, and roofs where indicated, not left as unbuilt outlines.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or wet room must be paired with a mirror (over or beside it) as part of the bathroom set; a basin without a mirror is an incomplete set.
Every kitchen worktop must carry a few real small appliances and decor pieces (kettle, toaster/coffee machine, board, fruit bowl), placed off the hob, sink and window.
A drawn terrace/balcony site area must be built as a slab with a guard before any door is allowed to open onto it; a door whose opening has no built deck is a defect.
A terrace must be built and reachable from outside before a drawn window is promoted to a terrace door; an un-built deck with a door on it is a defect.
An upper-floor opening that reaches a terrace must have a built deck and a guard; an un-built deck behind a door is a fall hazard.
An outside door must open onto a built, reachable deck or ground; a door whose target terrace is not built is an 'entrance to a window' defect.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or kitchen must carry a mirror mounted over or beside it; a basin left against a bare wall is incomplete.

When a site area (veranda, balcony, terrace) is drawn with a roof or eaves in the plan, the building stage must construct that roof slab and its supports; a columned outdoor space without its drawn roof is a loss, not a valid omission.

Outdoor-space columns must be sized to a slender structural proportion (not thick piers), and any balcony/veranda drawn with an adjacent sloped roof must have that sloped roof built, not a flat slab on heavy columns.

Every outside door that meets a level difference must be served by a designed entrance: solid-tread steps with cheek walls and a landing (or a ramp where accessibility asks), never a bare concrete stair with a thin handrail.
Every garden step must sit on its riser and the ground and be finished in the house's base stone or render with a coping; bare concrete treads in the grass are not acceptable.
Each outdoor floor must carry the material of its use (terrace, steps, path, drive) in one language with the house's base, never one bare slab everywhere.
Every outdoor room must be dressed for outside: no rug or carpet on its floor and only furniture made for outside (no upholstered indoor sofa or indoor table/chair).

the judge scores view ext_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The architecture is a clean, coherent massing, but the presentation is a grey-box placeholder, not a client-ready image. The reference sets a standard of rich material contrast (timber, stone, dark metal), a designed landscape, and warm, inviting light. This render has none of it: the lawn is a flat green plane, the trees are crude lollipops, the facade is a flat beige with no texture, and the interior is a dark void. A client would see a model, not a home.

missing layer: styled surfaces. The entire facade is a flat, untextured beige. The reference style demands a rich material palette (timber cladding, stone, dark metal) to create depth and a premium feel. This flatness makes the house look like a cardboard model.
also: missing layer: a place to sit. The ground-floor terrace is a bare, empty slab. The reference shows a designed outdoor living area. This one has no furniture, no planters, and no definition, making the main outdoor space feel useless and unfinished.

missing layer: a warm light. The render is lit by a flat, neutral, midday sun. There is no warm glow from the interior, no accent lighting on the facade, and no atmospheric quality. The house feels cold and dead, unlike the inviting, lived-in feel of the reference.

missing layer: planters. The landscape is a flat green void with no hardscaping, no planters, and no defined garden beds. The reference shows a designed landscape with paths and planting that frames the house. This one has none, which is a major presentation failure.

missing layer: material richness. The facade is a flat, untextured white surface. The reference style requires a mix of materials like wood cladding, stone, or textured panels to create depth and a premium feel.
missing layer: landscape styling. The ground is a flat green plane with no paths, planters, or hardscaping. The reference shows a designed garden with paved walkways and manicured lawns.

missing layer: architectural articulation. The roofline is a simple gable. The reference features complex roof forms, overhangs, and vertical elements that give the house a modern, designed character.
missing layer: exterior lighting. There are no wall sconces, path lights, or landscape lighting visible, which are essential for a modern exterior presentation.
missing layer: entrance definition. The main entrance is not clearly defined or highlighted. The reference has a distinct entry sequence with steps and a canopy.

missing layer: materiality and texture. The entire facade is a flat, untextured white surface. The reference style relies on a rich mix of cladding (wood, stone, tile) to create depth and a premium feel, which is completely absent here.

missing layer: a place to sit. The entrance area and the front yard are completely empty. The reference shows a defined entry path and a landscape that invites you in; this render has a blank void where a porch, seating, or even a simple planter should be.

missing layer: planters and landscaping. The site is a flat, uniform green plane with no garden beds, shrubs, or trees to ground the building. The reference uses a layered landscape to frame the house, while this render leaves the building floating in a void.

missing layer: lanterns and exterior lighting. There are no downlights, wall sconces, or path lights to define the entrance or the building's edges at night. The reference implies a well-lit, welcoming exterior, which is missing here.

missing layer: a rug or defined entry path. There is no material change on the ground to indicate a walkway or a landing area. The reference uses pavers to create a clear path, while this render has a single, unbroken lawn.
missing layer: planters; the terrace is a bare, empty slab with no planters or greenery to soften the hard edges and make the space feel lived-in.
missing layer: a place to sit; the large covered terrace is completely empty of furniture, failing to show the client how this key outdoor space is meant to be used.
missing layer: a rug; the outdoor floor is a single, unbroken material with no rug or mat to define a seating or dining zone.
missing layer: lanterns; the terrace and entrance have no outdoor lighting, making the space look dead and unusable after dark.
missing layer: a warm light; the entire scene is lit by a harsh, flat daylight with no warm accent lighting to create a welcoming atmosphere.
missing layer: styled surfaces; the facade is a flat, untextured beige with no material variation (stone, wood, metal) to give the house a sense of quality and design.
missing layer: a place to sit. The reference shows a defined outdoor living area; this render has a bare, flat lawn with no patio, deck, or furniture.
missing layer: planters. The reference uses structured planting and hardscape to frame the house; this render has none, just a flat green field.
missing layer: a path. There is no walkway or driveway leading to the entrance, leaving the house disconnected from its site.
missing layer: lanterns. The reference has exterior lighting to define the space at night; this render has no light fixtures.
The facade is a bare, untextured white surface. It lacks the material contrast (e.g., wood cladding, stone) seen in the reference, making it look like a placeholder.
The surrounding vegetation consists of crude, low-poly 'lollipop' trees that look like placeholders and do not contribute to a believable, designed landscape.

missing layer: planters. The terrace and facade are completely bare of greenery. The reference shows a lush, planted environment, while this render has a flat, empty lawn and no pots or planters to soften the hard architectural lines.
missing layer: a rug. The outdoor seating area on the wooden deck lacks a rug to define the zone and add texture, making the furniture look like it is just placed on the floor.

missing layer: cushions and throws. The outdoor sofa and chairs are bare. The reference style implies a comfortable, styled outdoor living space; these pieces need cushions and throws to look inviting and finished.

missing layer: a warm light. The scene is lit by harsh, flat daylight. There are no lanterns, string lights, or other warm light sources on the terrace or facade to create ambiance, especially for an evening view.

missing layer: styled surfaces. The terrace is empty except for the furniture. There are no side tables with decor, no outdoor lamps, and no other styling elements to make the space feel lived-in and designed.

findings.message: missing layer: curtains. The large upper-floor windows are dark, empty voids. Even in an exterior render, a hint of interior life (curtains, a lamp, a plant) is needed to make the house feel inhabited and to break up the flat black glass.

In the floor plan (Image 1), there is a large open terrace area to the north of the 'ebeveyn y odasi' and 'cocuk odasi' with a roof over it, but it lacks the necessary guardrails on all open edges and is not defined as a functional balcony in the model. It reads as a bare roof slab or an unfinished terrace rather than a usable balcony.

evidence.question: The balcony 'BALKON' (os_L1_balkon): from which door does a person step onto it; does every open edge over a drop have a guard; is it covered where a balcony should be (and where the roof plan covers it); does it read as a balcony (its floor, ceiling, posts, furniture, lights) or as something else (a carport, a bare slab, a roof)?
evidence.rule: Site areas labeled as 'BALKON' or 'VERANDA' in the plan must be built as functional outdoor rooms with floors, guards on open edges, and roofs where indicated, not left as unbuilt outlines.

lesson (lesson:UL31:L1): The L1 balcony is not built, so the terrace doors d_L1_001/d_L1_005 open onto an un-guarded drop; a person could fall out of the upper-floor opening.

findings.message: lesson (lesson:UL82): The entrance is met by a short flight of bare concrete steps with a thin metal handrail and no cheek walls, no landing, and no stone coping; the terrace is a single flat slab and the garden is flat grass with no terracing, banks or planted edges.

evidence.question: Does the garden meet every level difference as a landscape architect would build it: banks of at most 1:3 / 1:2, terraces at one level per side and planted, flights of solid treads with cheek walls and a landing, paths level across and stepped where steeper than 1:12, a ramp only where accessibility asks, walls in the house's base stone with a coping?
evidence.rule: Every outside door that meets a level difference must be served by a designed entrance: solid-tread steps with cheek walls and a landing (or a ramp where accessibility asks), never a bare concrete stair with a thin handrail.

also: lesson (lesson:UL83): The entrance steps are bare concrete treads sitting on the grass with no stone or render finish and no coping; the retaining/plinth is the only stone element and the steps themselves are unfinished concrete.

rules_proposed.rule: Dressing rooms must include a dressing table or vanity group with accessories (mirror, stool, decor) to satisfy the 'styled surfaces' requirement; a wardrobe alone is insufficient.
Bedrooms should have a feature wall (e.g., slatted wood, paneling) behind the bed to add visual interest and match the reference style.
Nightstands in master bedrooms must be styled with accessories (books, vases, art) to avoid looking bare.
Living rooms must include a large area rug under the seating group to anchor the space.
Bedrooms should have a feature wall (e.g., paneling) behind the bed to add visual interest.
Bathroom cameras must show the main fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) to demonstrate the room's function and style.
Bathtub surrounds should use warm wood tones to match the project's aesthetic, not dark untextured panels.
Bathroom walls should use large-format porcelain tiles or stone to create a cohesive, high-end look, not flat cold white tiles.
Bathroom cameras must show the vanity unit and mirror to capture the room's style.
Kitchen cameras must show the kitchen run, island, and appliances, not just the dining nook.
Kitchen cameras must focus on the kitchen functional group, not the dining table.

A kitchen's program must include a styled-surface layer (small decor on the counter and island: a kettle, a fruit bowl, a cutting board) placed by the furniture agent, not only the functional run; a bare counter is a failed kitchen render.
A bathroom's program must include a mirror above the washbasin; a bare wall above the basin is a failed bathroom render.
A bedroom window's program must include a full-height two-layer curtain treatment (sheer behind a heavier drape) on a ceiling track; a single short sheer panel is a failed bedroom render.
A bedroom window's program must include a full-height two-layer curtain treatment (sheer behind a heavier drape) on a ceiling track; a single flat white panel is a failed bedroom render.
An interior camera of a small wet room must be posed from a free point with headroom that shows the room's main fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), never from a corner framing a wall and a door leaf.
A second interior view of a small room must frame the room as a whole, not a close-up of one fixture.
Two armchairs placed as a pair in one room must share a coherent style and palette; when they do not, swap the one that breaks the set to a model that matches its partner.

A piece listed in a room's program that is 'not built' must be built (or the room re-laid out) before the room is judged; a bare wall where a drawn work set belongs is a missing piece, not a styling gap.
An interior camera of a hall must show the hall's functional furniture (shoe cabinet, bench, console), not a bare blank wall.
A hall's entrance group is not complete with only a shoe cabinet; the furniture agent must add the missing styled layer (bench, hooks, mirror) that the reference shows.
An interior camera of a small hall must show the console and the space, not be jammed into the corner between the door and a wall.
A bed's layered bedding (duvet, second blanket, euro shams, decorative cushion) is a styling layer the furniture agent must add; a model swap that lowers the rating is not the fix.
Windows in a furnished bedroom must carry layered curtains (sheer plus drape on a track); bare windows are a missing styling layer the furniture agent must add.
Nightstands and dressers in a furnished bedroom must carry styled surfaces (vase, books, mirror, leaning art); bare tops are a missing styling layer the furniture agent must add.
An interior camera of a small room must show the room's main furniture and layout, not be pressed against a door and a wardrobe edge.
A second interior view of a small room must show the room and its furniture, not a close-up of a wall corner and door edge.
null
A parametric opening in the style's finish is an acceptable build when no library model of the building's window family fits the opening's dimensions; it is not a defect.

When a piece is built with a parametric mesh because no library model fits, the fitting stage must record the piece's room and id so that a later swap_model or retype can target it; otherwise the library gap is unfixable by the agent.
A kitchen counter or island in a furnished render should carry at least one small appliance or decor item to avoid reading as an unfinished worktop.
A shower in a bathroom render should have a clear glass screen or proper tiling definition; a flat, untextured surface reads as a placeholder.
Nightstands in a bedroom should match the wood tone of the room's feature wall panelling to avoid introducing a clashing third wood tone.
A bedroom in a furnished render should have at least two layers of light (e.g., a statement fixture over the bed plus bedside lamps) to match the project's style.
Doors in a furnished render should have a wood tone and hardware that match the project's style; plain flat slabs with a single handle read as generic wardrobes.
A hall in a furnished render should have a rug to ground the space and add warmth, especially when the reference shows one.
Doors in a furnished render should have a wood tone and hardware that match the project's style; plain flat slabs in a pale wood read as generic placeholders.

A wardrobe model whose doors render as flat, untextured colour blocks is a low-quality asset: swap it for a library model of the same family with real door material, never move the piece to hide the look.

A facade that reads as flat planes with simple reveals needs a material with real surface breaks (render/plaster with texture, or a cladding) rather than a single flat colour; set the facade slot to a textured exterior look.
An interior camera must frame the room's layout and its main pieces, not be pressed against a door leaf or furniture edge at a low angle.
An exterior view must frame the main facade, entrance and the house's scale at eye level (1.5-1.7 m), not a corner of the roof and a hedge from too high and too far.
Every room must have a visible floor finish that matches the project's style.
The outdoor view through windows must show a believable environment with trees, ground cover, and site elements, not a low-poly placeholder.
A child's room must have wall art (murals, posters, or art) to match the reference style.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood, textured stone, and functional styling (mirror, towel rail) to match the project's style.
A bathroom must have a mirror over the basin to match the reference style.
A bathtub's model must match the project's light, minimalist aesthetic.
Bathroom renders must show warm wood textures, a vanity unit, a mirror, and a towel rail to match the project's style.
Kitchen renders must show styling and 'lived-in' layers to match the reference, not a raw architectural model.

A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a cohesive, age-appropriate set (playful, warm, child-sized); a generic adult office or minimalist set is a mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping the models to a matching style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a generic adult bedroom is a failure of the furniture set, not the camera.
A modern white office chair is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate chair that matches the room's style.
A minimalist white-framed office desk is not a valid piece for a child's bedroom; the furniture agent must replace it with a child-appropriate desk that matches the room's style.
A render of a child's room must show a playful, warm, child-appropriate interior; a cluttered adult bedroom with clashing furniture is a failure of the furniture set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a wall showing a bare corner is a bad camera.
A nightstand in a master bedroom must match the room's warm, organic style; a loud, artificial object (e.g. a neon lamp) that clashes with the natural wood and neutral palette is a mismatch.
An armchair in a master bedroom must match the room's organic, boho style; a mid-century modern piece that clashes with the natural wood elements is a mismatch.
A render of a master bedroom must show a warm, organic, and layered interior; a sterile, unfinished shell with clashing surfaces is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A master bedroom must be lit with warm, cozy light; a flat, cool ambient light that feels like a hospital ward is a failure of the lighting and material set.
A render of a hall must show a warm, textured, and functionally styled interior; a bare, empty shell with no console table or decor is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A hall must have styled surfaces (console table, decor, and a rug); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main functional group; a camera pressed against a door leaf is a bad camera.
A storage room must have styled surfaces (hanging clothes, a mirror, etc.); a bare, empty corner with no styling is a failure of the furniture and material set.
A bedroom under 12 m2 that the solver cannot relayout still gets one potted_plant in a corner the solver leaves free, so the room is never rendered bare.
When the current bed model is a blocky placeholder and a generated model of the same type and style is available, swap to the generated model rather than leaving the placeholder.
A bedroom render that shows only blocky furniture and flat walls is a fit failure: the furniture agent must add at least one plant, one textile and one wall item before the view is scored.
An interior camera that frames only a door and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe is missing its program: the furniture agent must add a mirror, a bench and wall art so the room reads as a dressing room, not a storage closet.
A room whose walls are completely bare in the render is missing the wall-art layer: the furniture agent must add at least one framed piece on a free wall span.
An interior camera that frames only a wall corner and a fixture edge is a camera failure: the camera must be moved to a free point that shows the room's main pieces, not a fragment.
A facade that renders as a flat white box is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look (wood, stone, or brick) that matches the project's reference style.
A ground-floor plinth with no planters, shrubs or ground cover is a site failure: the site must include planters and a hedge or fence to soften the transition to the lawn.
A facade that renders as a bare clay model is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A facade that renders as a flat untextured white surface is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
An exterior wall with no place to sit is a site failure: the site must include a patio set or bench to make the exterior feel lived-in.
An exterior wall with no lanterns, wall sconces or path lights is a site failure: the site must include exterior lighting to define the space at night.
A facade that renders as a grey-box massing study is a material failure: the facade slot must carry a cladding look that matches the project's reference style.
A house with outside doors but no library entrance door is a build failure: the build stage must assign a statement entrance door model to the entrance opening.

When an interior door is drawn as a double and the library holds no double-leaf model, build it parametric in the style's finish and record a library_gap; do not force a single-leaf model onto a double opening.

A piece whose room is None (orphaned, not assigned to a room) cannot be refitted or swapped; the fitting stage must assign every placed piece to a room before the library-quality check, or the check must skip orphaned pieces instead of flagging them.

When two interior doors in the same tight space (hall, corridor) are built from the same heavy traditional model, the fitting stage should vary at least one to a lighter or different-style model from the library to avoid a dated, repetitive look.

rules_proposed.rule: Every room must be reachable from the entrance through doors, openings, or stairs.
Every floor must be reachable from the entrance.

A piece that blocks the ray through a window or door opening is a placement error: the fitting stage must keep the clear zone of every opening free of furniture, or move the piece to the nearest free spot.
A washbasin in a bathroom is always accompanied by a mirror above it; the bathroom_set group must include a mirror as a mandatory member.
A door leaf must be built with its frame and threshold at the correct floor level; a floating door leaf indicates a missing frame or a level mismatch in the door builder.
A site area marked 'NOT built (no outline)' that is referenced by a door or window in the plan must be built as an outdoor space with a floor slab and guard rails; the site stage must not skip it.
A kitchen must have a continuous run of base cabinets, wall cabinets, and appliances; the kitchen_run group must be placed as a single unit.
A door that opens onto an outdoor space must have that outdoor space built; the site stage must build the balcony or terrace before the door is placed.
The garden must include planted beds, shrubs, ground cover, and a path or parking area; the site stage must not leave it as bare flat grass.
A veranda or balcony marked 'NOT built (no outline)' must be built with a floor slab, guard rails, and a roof if drawn; the site stage must not skip it.
An entrance door must have a proper approach with steps, a landing, and cheek walls; the site stage must build the entrance solution.
A door that is blocked by furniture and has no outside passage is a reading error; it should be read as a window at the floor's sill height.
A ray through a window opening must not hit furniture: the build stage must clear any piece that blocks the way through an opening.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a bare bowl with no mirror is a fundamental design failure.
A bathroom's washbasin must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the bathroom but misses the basin is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A bathroom washbasin must be part of a complete bathroom set (basin, mirror, vanity or at least a mirror above it); a basin with no mirror over it is a fundamental design failure.
A small enclosed room (under 3 m2) with no function, no pieces and no door of its own is most likely a misread: it is a hall or passage, not a room of its own, and must be typed accordingly.
A dressing room (Soyunma Odası) must contain at least a mirror and a bench or seating in addition to a wardrobe to be functionally complete; a single wardrobe is insufficient for the room type.
Site areas labeled as 'BALKON' or 'VERANDA' in the plan must be built as functional outdoor rooms with floors, guards on open edges, and roofs where indicated, not left as unbuilt outlines.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or wet room must be paired with a mirror (over or beside it) as part of the bathroom set; a basin without a mirror is an incomplete set.
Every kitchen worktop must carry a few real small appliances and decor pieces (kettle, toaster/coffee machine, board, fruit bowl), placed off the hob, sink and window.
A drawn terrace/balcony site area must be built as a slab with a guard before any door is allowed to open onto it; a door whose opening has no built deck is a defect.
A terrace must be built and reachable from outside before a drawn window is promoted to a terrace door; an un-built deck with a door on it is a defect.
An upper-floor opening that reaches a terrace must have a built deck and a guard; an un-built deck behind a door is a fall hazard.
An outside door must open onto a built, reachable deck or ground; a door whose target terrace is not built is an 'entrance to a window' defect.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or kitchen must carry a mirror mounted over or beside it; a basin left against a bare wall is incomplete.

When a site area (veranda, balcony, terrace) is drawn with a roof or eaves in the plan, the building stage must construct that roof slab and its supports; a columned outdoor space without its drawn roof is a loss, not a valid omission.

Outdoor-space columns must be sized to a slender structural proportion (not thick piers), and any balcony/veranda drawn with an adjacent sloped roof must have that sloped roof built, not a flat slab on heavy columns.

Every outside door that meets a level difference must be served by a designed entrance: solid-tread steps with cheek walls and a landing (or a ramp where accessibility asks), never a bare concrete stair with a thin handrail.
Every garden step must sit on its riser and the ground and be finished in the house's base stone or render with a coping; bare concrete treads in the grass are not acceptable.
Each outdoor floor must carry the material of its use (terrace, steps, path, drive) in one language with the house's base, never one bare slab everywhere.
Every outdoor room must be dressed for outside: no rug or carpet on its floor and only furniture made for outside (no upholstered indoor sofa or indoor table/chair).

guards: sense (N*: every room reached, no bathroom as a corridor, every level reached; a stair joins the room it starts in and the room it arrives in)
model review (M*; M9: the walk from every stair into the rooms, to every door; M15: the stair's handrails as one balustrade, no rail crossing another or stopping short)
architect rules (K4: a cut-off stair takes the reading that leads into its floors)

rules_proposed.rule: An interior room camera must frame the room's defining functional group (a kitchen's run and island, a bedroom's bed) so the room reads as its type, not as a generic or secondary zone.

A stair piece must be assigned to a hall or dedicated stairwell room, never to a kitchen or other habitable room; the reading stage must re-assign a stair found inside a kitchen to the nearest hall or stairwell.
A bathroom fixture listed in the room's pieces but absent from the render must be given a real library model (not a parametric mesh) so it is built and visible.
A bathroom camera that points at a corner and misses the primary fixtures (washbasin, toilet) must be re-aimed to show the main function of the space.
A bathroom camera that misses the primary fixtures (shower, toilet, basin) must be re-aimed to show the main function of the space.
A dressing room camera that cuts off the main furniture (wardrobes) and shows no defining pieces must be re-aimed to show the space's function.

A stair read into a kitchen (or any room where a stair does not belong) must be re-read as the missing kitchen fixture (fridge) if its size and position match, or removed if it is a misread symbol, rather than being left as a stair in the kitchen.
A door read from its lines (no swing arc) in an outer wall that is blocked by a drawn piece (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall that is blocked by drawn pieces (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A door read from its lines (no swing arc) in an outer wall that is blocked by drawn pieces (no passage) must be re-read as a window at the floor's sill.
A door read from lines without a swing arc in an outer wall, whose approach is blocked by furniture, is a window at the floor's sill, not a door.
A gap in an outer wall blocked by furniture is a window, not a door.
A wall cabinet must not be placed over a window; if no free wall span exists, it must be removed or the window moved.
Furniture must not cover a window opening.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished with its defining set (bench, full-length mirror, open storage or hanger rail); a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room and the room's program must be completed, not just re-modelled.

A room's main group (dining table and its chairs) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main group is a camera failure, not a model failure.
A room's main piece (a hall's console table) must be visible in at least one of the room's cameras; a camera that frames the room but misses its main piece is a camera failure, not a model failure.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between them (a wall not read) so each label keeps its own room; the label with the largest printed area is kept only as a fallback.
A room's furniture must read as a designed space, not a collection of pieces; the furniture stage must keep the room's function clear (a bedroom is not an office).
A piece must look like its type in every view; the fit stage must choose a model whose silhouette matches the type (a bed_double must not read as a bed_single).
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position.
A built piece must sit within 0.05 m of its drawn place and match its drawn size; the layout stage must place it at its drawn position and size.
An outer-wall opening whose approach is fully blocked by a drawn counter or fixture is a window, not a door: the reading must classify it by what stands in front of it, not by its width.
A wall unit must not stand over a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the unit to a free wall span.
A piece must not cover a window; the fit must check the window's span and move the piece to a free spot.

A standard bedroom-set piece (nightstand) that is left unbuilt because it cuts a neighbour is a loss of a drawn element: the sleeping group is re-solved as one unit around its drawn anchor so the nightstand is built, not dropped for a spatial conflict.
